Related-work section:
Transformers have been widely adopted for time series analysis, though their efficacy is scrutinized. *Are Transformers Effective for Time Series Forecasting?* questions the validity of Transformer-based solutions for long-term forecasting, while *Transformers in Time Series: A Survey* documents challenges in time series analysis and *Out-of-Distribution Generalization in Time Series: A Survey* documents the growing interest and the challenges of distribution shifts in this domain [5, 15, 14]. Specific adaptations include *Knowledge Aggregation Transformer Network for Multivariate Time Series Classification*, which utilizes dual networks for feature extraction, and *Domain Adaptation for Time series Transformers using One-step fine-tuning*, which addresses prediction limitations through fine-tuning [7, 12]. These works establish the context of Transformer application but do not isolate FFN weight geometry as a variable for subject-disjoint generalization.

Research specifically targeting the Feed-Forward Network (FFN) component examines structural design and capacity control. *Investigating the Role of Feed-Forward Networks in Transformers Using Parallel Attention and Feed-Forward Net Design* compares parallel versus series attention and FFN designs to understand their key roles [11]. *FL-Tuning: Layer Tuning for Feed-Forward Network in Transformer* explores tuning FFN layers for downstream tasks, and *An Efficient Two-Stage Pipelined Compute-in-Memory Macro for Accelerating Transformer Feed-Forward Networks* focuses on hardware acceleration for these components [13, 10]. Foundational work such as *Regularization and complexity control in feed-forward networks* considers approaches like architecture selection and training with noise for complexity control [6]. Together, these papers establish that FFN capacity and design are adjustable levers, but they do not test weight norm variance regularization for generalization.

Regarding regularization and generalization strategies, several studies test weight geometry and consistency constraints. *Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning* tests whether enforcing a low-entropy singular value spectrum on input projection weights enhances held-out classification accuracy [4]. *Weight-Sharing Regularization* proposes a penalty on weight differences to encourage sharing [9]. In the context of subject-disjoint generalization, *Cross-Layer Query Consistency Loss Tests Whether Attention Stability Across Depth Improves Subject-Disjoint Generalization in Time-Series Transformers* tests enforcing consistency in attention query projections [2]. However, *Replication: Cross-Layer Query Consistency Loss Tests Whether Attention Stability Across Depth Improves Subject-Disjoint Generalization in Time-Series Transformers* discloses inconclusive decisions [1]. Additionally, *Entropy-Maximized Multiplicative Weight Noise for Subject-Disjoint Robustness* carries a retracted notice from the journal, although its abstract states the numerical outputs are computationally reproducible [3]. These findings position the current study against a backdrop of inconclusive or retracted results, motivating a rigorous test of FFN neuron capacity balancing.

Central to the effectiveness of PAF are two main assumptions regarding the FFN block and the attention block within a layer: 1) the primary function of the FFN block is to maintain isotropy among token embeddings and prevent their degeneration, and 2) the residual norm computed in the attention block is substantially smaller than the input token embedding norm. To empirically validate these assumptions, we train PAF variants of two large language models (RoBERTa-large and bert-large-uncased). Our results demonstrate that both assumptions hold true in the PAF design. This study contributes to a deeper understanding of the roles and interactions between FFNs and self-attention mechanisms in transformer architectures.

[12] Domain Adaptation for Time series Transformers using One-step fine-tuning
Abstract: The recent breakthrough of Transformers in deep learning has drawn significant attention of the time series community due to their ability to capture long-range dependencies. However, like other deep learning models, Transformers face limitations in time series prediction, including insufficient temporal understanding, generalization challenges, and data shift issues for the domains with limited data. Additionally, addressing the issue of catastrophic forgetting, where models forget previously learned information when exposed to new data, is another critical aspect that requires attention in enhancing the robustness of Transformers for time series tasks. To address these limitations, in this paper, we pre-train the time series Transformer model on a source domain with sufficient data and fine-tune it on the target domain with limited data. We introduce the \emph{One-step fine-tuning} approach, adding some percentage of source domain data to the target domains, providing the model with diverse time series instances. We then fine-tune the pre-trained model using a gradual unfreezing technique. This helps enhance the model's performance in time series prediction for domains with limited data. Extensive experimental results on two real-world datasets show that our approach improves over the state-of-the-art baselines by 4.35% and 11.54% for indoor temperature and wind power prediction, respectively.

[13] FL-Tuning: Layer Tuning for Feed-Forward Network in Transformer
Abstract: Prompt tuning is an emerging way of adapting pre-trained language models to downstream tasks. However, the existing studies are mainly to add prompts to the input sequence. This way would not work as expected due to the intermediate multi-head self-attention and feed-forward network computation, making model optimization not very smooth. Hence, we propose a novel tuning way called layer tuning, aiming to add learnable parameters in Transformer layers. Specifically, we focus on layer tuning for feed-forward network in the Transformer, namely FL-tuning. It introduces additional units into the hidden layer of each feed-forward network. We conduct extensive experiments on the public CLUE benchmark. The results show that: 1) Our FL-tuning outperforms prompt tuning methods under both full-data and few-shot settings in almost all cases. In particular, it improves accuracy by 17.93% (full-data setting) on WSC 1.0 and F1 by 16.142% (few-shot setting) on CLUENER over P-tuning v2. 2) Our FL-tuning is more stable and converges about 1.17 times faster than P-tuning v2. 3) With only about 3% of Transformer's parameters to be trained, FL-tuning is comparable with fine-tuning on most datasets, and significantly outperforms fine-tuning (e.g., accuracy improved by 12.9% on WSC 1.1) on several datasets. The source codes are available at https://github.com/genggui001/FL-Tuning.

[14] Out-of-Distribution Generalization in Time Series: A Survey
Abstract: Time series frequently manifest distribution shifts, diverse latent features, and non-stationary learning dynamics, particularly in open and evolving environments. These characteristics pose significant challenges for out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization. While substantial progress has been made, a systematic synthesis of advancements remains lacking. To address this gap, we present the first comprehensive review of OOD generalization methodologies for time series, organized to delineate the field's evolutionary trajectory and contemporary research landscape. We organize our analysis across three foundational dimensions: data distribution, representation learning, and OOD evaluation. For each dimension, we present several popular algorithms in detail. Furthermore, we highlight key application scenarios, emphasizing their real-world impact. Finally, we identify persistent challenges and propose future research directions. A detailed summary of the methods reviewed for the generalization of OOD in time series can be accessed at https://tsood-generalization.com.

[15] Transformers in Time Series: A Survey
Abstract: Transformers have achieved superior performances in many tasks in natural language processing and computer vision, which also triggered great interest in the time series community. Among multiple advantages of Transformers, the ability to capture long-range dependencies and interactions is especially attractive for time series modeling, leading to exciting progress in various time series applications. In this paper, we systematically review Transformer schemes for time series modeling by highlighting their strengths as well as limitations. In particular, we examine the development of time series Transformers in two perspectives. From the perspective of network structure, we summarize the adaptations and modifications that have been made to Transformers in order to accommodate the challenges in time series analysis. From the perspective of applications, we categorize time series Transformers based on common tasks including forecasting, anomaly detection, and classification. Empirically, we perform robust analysis, model size analysis, and seasonal-trend decomposition analysis to study how Transformers perform in time series. Finally, we discuss and suggest future directions to provide useful research guidance. To the best of our knowledge, this paper is the first work to comprehensively and systematically summarize the recent advances of Transformers for modeling time series data. We hope this survey will ignite further research interests in time series Transformers.

messages.content: You are a meticulous citation fact-checker. You are given a related-work section and the abstracts of the papers it cites. Identify any claim attributed to a cited paper that is NOT supported by that paper's abstract — misattribution, overstated findings, or fabricated results. Judge only against the abstracts provided.

Related-work section:
Transformers have been widely adopted for time series analysis, though their efficacy is scrutinized. *Are Transformers Effective for Time Series Forecasting?* questions the validity of Transformer-based solutions for long-term forecasting, while *Transformers in Time Series: A Survey* documents challenges in time series analysis and *Out-of-Distribution Generalization in Time Series: A Survey* documents the growing interest and the challenges of distribution shifts in this domain [5, 15, 14]. Specific adaptations include *Knowledge Aggregation Transformer Network for Multivariate Time Series Classification*, which utilizes dual networks for feature extraction, and *Domain Adaptation for Time series Transformers using One-step fine-tuning*, which addresses prediction limitations through fine-tuning [7, 12]. These works establish the context of Transformer application but do not isolate FFN weight geometry as a variable for subject-disjoint generalization.

Research specifically targeting the Feed-Forward Network (FFN) component examines structural design and capacity control. *Investigating the Role of Feed-Forward Networks in Transformers Using Parallel Attention and Feed-Forward Net Design* compares parallel versus series attention and FFN designs to understand their key roles [11]. *FL-Tuning: Layer Tuning for Feed-Forward Network in Transformer* explores tuning FFN layers for downstream tasks, and *An Efficient Two-Stage Pipelined Compute-in-Memory Macro for Accelerating Transformer Feed-Forward Networks* focuses on hardware acceleration for these components [13, 10]. Foundational work such as *Regularization and complexity control in feed-forward networks* considers approaches like architecture selection and training with noise for complexity control [6]. Together, these papers establish that FFN capacity and design are adjustable levers, but they do not test weight norm variance regularization for generalization.

Regarding regularization and generalization strategies, several studies test weight geometry and consistency constraints. *Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning* tests whether enforcing a low-entropy singular value spectrum on input projection weights enhances held-out classification accuracy [4]. *Weight-Sharing Regularization* proposes a penalty on weight differences to encourage sharing [9]. In the context of subject-disjoint generalization, *Cross-Layer Query Consistency Loss Tests Whether Attention Stability Across Depth Improves Subject-Disjoint Generalization in Time-Series Transformers* tests enforcing consistency in attention query projections [2]. However, *Replication: Cross-Layer Query Consistency Loss Tests Whether Attention Stability Across Depth Improves Subject-Disjoint Generalization in Time-Series Transformers* discloses inconclusive decisions [1]. Additionally, *Entropy-Maximized Multiplicative Weight Noise for Subject-Disjoint Robustness* carries a retracted notice from the journal, although its abstract states the numerical outputs are computationally reproducible [3]. These findings position the current study against a backdrop of inconclusive or retracted results, motivating a rigorous test of FFN neuron capacity balancing.

Cited papers and their abstracts:
[1] Replication: Cross-Layer Query Consistency Loss Tests Whether Attention Stability Across Depth Improves Subject-Disjoint Generalization in Time-Series Transformers
Abstract: [EDITORIAL NOTICE — ERRATUM: this paper carries a erratum notice from the journal that published it. Stated reason: Version 2. It discloses the independent reproduction: the re-run on different GPU hardware confirmed both registered inconclusive decisions, its per-seed results were not numerically identical, and its confirmatory-replication interval excludes zero. No registered result changed. This version adds a reproduction disclosure to the Limitations section, and corrects 2 sentences in the Related Work section so that each citation is attributed to the work that supports it. No other section, reference, figure or table differs from the previous version; CORRECTION.md shows every changed sentence.. Its conclusions may not be relied on; cite it only with its status stated.] Transformers are increasingly applied to time-series analysis, yet whether architectural inductive biases improve subject-disjoint generalization remains unclear. This replication study tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projection weights improves held-out classification accuracy compared to standard training. We employed a PreNormTransformerEncoder on the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset with an official subject-disjoint split. The intervention added a Frobenius norm consistency loss regularizing deeper block query projections toward earlier blocks. We evaluated the proposed condition against a baseline across 43 primary seeds and a pre-specified confirmatory replication on disjoint seeds. In the primary cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.00077 (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436], p=0.657). In the replication cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.00196 (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571], p=0.331). Confidence intervals in both cohorts included zero, and neither exceeded the preregistered worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion. The results are inconclusive. These findings suggest that cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime. This experiment did not test whether layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks.

[2] Cross-Layer Query Consistency Loss Tests Whether Attention Stability Across Depth Improves Subject-Disjoint Generalization in Time-Series Transformers
Abstract: Transformers have become prominent in time-series analysis, yet whether architectural inductive biases improve subject-disjoint generalization remains unclear. This study tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy compared to standard training. We employed a PreNormTransformerEncoder on the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset with an official subject-disjoint split. The intervention added a Frobenius norm consistency loss regularizing deeper block projections toward earlier blocks. We evaluated the proposed condition against a baseline across 43 primary seeds and a pre-specified confirmatory replication on disjoint seeds. In the primary cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.00133 (95% CI [-0.00315, 0.0056], p=0.546). In the replication cohort, the proposed condition worsened accuracy by -0.00157 (95% CI [-0.00487, 0.00182], p=0.372). Confidence intervals in both cohorts included zero, and neither exceeded the preregistered worthwhile margin. Variation across observations is attributed to the seeds that produced them. The results are inconclusive. These findings suggest that cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime, indicating layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks.

[3] Entropy-Maximized Multiplicative Weight Noise for Subject-Disjoint Robustness
Abstract: [EDITORIAL NOTICE — RETRACTED: this paper carries a retracted notice from the journal that published it. Stated reason: The numerical outputs reported in this paper remain computationally reproducible: an independent re-run from the archived reproducibility bundle reproduced all eight aggregate metrics within tolerance. A post-publication audit of the artifact source found that the executed intervention did not implement the preregistered intervention. The preregistration committed to a multiplicative weight perturbation applied BEFORE the forward pass, an entropy term added to the training OBJECTIVE, and a noise scale learned by BACKPROPAGATION, with held-out evaluation on the clean weights. The experiment har. Its conclusions may not be relied on; cite it only with its status stated.] Uncertainty quantification in deep learning is critical for robust deployment, yet standard deterministic training often fails to provide calibrated confidence under distribution shift. This study investigates whether explicitly maximizing the entropy of multiplicative weight noise parameters during training improves out-of-distribution accuracy on subject-disjoint time-series data compared to standard deterministic training. We preregistered a hypothesis that entropy maximization would yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the baseline, exceeding a fixed worthwhile margin. Using a Transformer architecture on the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset with an official subject-disjoint split, we evaluated the intervention across 43 primary and 43 confirmatory-replication seeds. The results refuted the preregistered hypothesis in both cohorts. In the primary cohort, the proposed condition worsened accuracy by 0.04805 proportion (95% CI [-0.0714, -0.0324], p=0.0002) relative to the baseline. The replication cohort confirmed this degradation with a contrast of -0.03482 (95% CI [-0.0422, -0.0278], p=0.0002). Negative controls involving entropy minimization and fixed noise performed comparably to the deterministic baseline. These findings indicate that entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters does not generalize to attention-based architectures under distribution shift and may actively impair performance. Practitioners should prioritize standard regularization over explicit entropy maximization for robustness tasks in this regime.

[4] Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning
Abstract: Regularization design for temporal feature learning often assumes specific weight geometries facilitate generalization under distribution shift. This study tests whether enforcing a low-entropy singular value spectrum on input projection weights enhances held-out classification accuracy compared to standard weight decay in a subject-disjoint time-series setting. We preregistered a hypothesis that the intervention would exceed a fixed worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion in accuracy gain. Using a Transformer architecture on the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset, we evaluated the proposed condition against a baseline and two negative controls across 43 primary and 43 confirmatory-replication seeds. The results were inconclusive: the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.0004419 (95% CI [-0.00213, 0.0031], p=0.75) in the primary cohort and 0.002549 (95% CI [-0.000331, 0.0055], p=0.106) in the replication cohort. Neither estimate exceeded the preregistered margin, and confidence intervals included zero. These findings suggest that spectral entropy minimization of input projections does not yield robust accuracy gains over standard weight decay in this regime. We report these null results to clarify the mechanistic role of weight spectra in finite-width networks.

[5] Are Transformers Effective for Time Series Forecasting?
Abstract: Recently, there has been a surge of Transformer-based solutions for the long-term time series forecasting (LTSF) task. Despite the growing performance over the past few years, we question the validity of this line of research in this work. Specifically, Transformers is arguably the most successful solution to extract the semantic correlations among the elements in a long sequence. However, in time series modeling, we are to extract the temporal relations in an ordered set of continuous points. While employing positional encoding and using tokens to embed sub-series in Transformers facilitate preserving some ordering information, the nature of the permutation-invariant self-attention mechanism inevitably results in temporal information loss. To validate our claim, we introduce a set of embarrassingly simple one-layer linear models named LTSF-Linear for comparison. Experimental results on nine real-life datasets show that LTSF-Linear surprisingly outperforms existing sophisticated Transformer-based LTSF models in all cases, and often by a large margin. Moreover, we conduct comprehensive empirical studies to explore the impacts of various design elements of LTSF models on their temporal relation extraction capability. We hope this surprising finding opens up new research directions for the LTSF task. We also advocate revisiting the validity of Transformer-based solutions for other time series analysis tasks (e.g., anomaly detection) in the future.

[6] Regularization and complexity control in feed-forward networks
Abstract: In this paper we consider four alternative approaches to complexity control in feed-forward networks based respectively on architecture selection, regularization, early stopping, and training with noise. We show that there are close similarities between these approaches and we argue that, for most practical applications, the technique of regularization should be the method of choice.

[7] Knowledge Aggregation Transformer Network for Multivariate Time Series Classification
Abstract: Over the years, various sophisticated deep learning algorithms have surfaced for multivariate time series classification (MTSC), notably the dual-network-based model. This model comprises two parallel networks tailored to time series data: one for local feature extraction and the other for global relation extraction. However, effectively integrating these dual networks poses a significant challenge. To address this, we propose a knowledge aggregation transformer network (KATN) for MTSC. KATN, composed of four aggregation transformer blocks, extracts abundant regularizations and connections hidden within the data. Each block incorporates a modified residual network (MResNet) for local feature extraction and a multi-head attention network for global relation extraction. Initially, the block merges MResNet's output feature with that of the multi-head attention network through an additive operation. Subsequently, it aligns features with a fully connected (i.e., dense) layer and activates neural units using the Gaussian error linear unit function. This strategic feature aggregation allows for capturing long-range dependencies among multiple variables in multivariate time series data. Experimental results demonstrate that KATN significantly outperforms 6 state-of-the-art transformer variants, achieving a ‘win’/‘tie’/‘lose’ record of 9/6/15 and securing the lowest AVG_rank score. Furthermore, when evaluated against 18 existing MTSC algorithms across 13 UEA datasets, KATN consistently delivers superior performance, attaining the lowest AVG_rank score among all compared methods.

[8] AdaCap: Adaptive Capacity control for Feed-Forward Neural Networks
Abstract: The capacity of a ML model refers to the range of functions this model can approximate. It impacts both the complexity of the patterns a model can learn but also memorization, the ability of a model to fit arbitrary labels. We propose Adaptive Capacity (AdaCap), a training scheme for Feed-Forward Neural Networks (FFNN). AdaCap optimizes the capacity of FFNN so it can capture the high-level abstract representations underlying the problem at hand without memorizing the training dataset. AdaCap is the combination of two novel ingredients, the Muddling labels for Regularization (MLR) loss and the Tikhonov operator training scheme. The MLR loss leverages randomly generated labels to quantify the propensity of a model to memorize. We prove that the MLR loss is an accurate in-sample estimator for out-of-sample generalization performance and that it can be used to perform Hyper-Parameter Optimization provided a Signal-to-Noise Ratio condition is met. The Tikhonov operator training scheme modulates the capacity of a FFNN in an adaptive, differentiable and data-dependent manner. We assess the effectiveness of AdaCap in a setting where DNN are typically prone to memorization, small tabular datasets, and benchmark its performance against popular machine learning methods.

[9] Weight-Sharing Regularization
Abstract: Weight-sharing is ubiquitous in deep learning. Motivated by this, we propose a "weight-sharing regularization" penalty on the weights $w \in \mathbb{R}^d$ of a neural network, defined as $\mathcal{R}(w) = \frac{1}{d - 1}\sum_{i > j}^d |w_i - w_j|$. We study the proximal mapping of $\mathcal{R}$ and provide an intuitive interpretation of it in terms of a physical system of interacting particles. We also parallelize existing algorithms for $\operatorname{prox}_\mathcal{R}$ (to run on GPU) and find that one of them is fast in practice but slow ($O(d)$) for worst-case inputs. Using the physical interpretation, we design a novel parallel algorithm which runs in $O(\log^3 d)$ when sufficient processors are available, thus guaranteeing fast training. Our experiments reveal that weight-sharing regularization enables fully connected networks to learn convolution-like filters even when pixels have been shuffled while convolutional neural networks fail in this setting. Our code is available on github.

[10] An Efficient Two-Stage Pipelined Compute-in-Memory Macro for Accelerating Transformer Feed-Forward Networks
Abstract: Transformer architectures have achieved state-of-the-art performance in various applications. However, deploying transformer models on resource-constrained platforms is still challenging due to its dynamic workloads, intensive computations, and substantial memory access. In this article, we propose a two-stage pipelined compute-in-memory (CIM) macro for effectively deploying and accelerating the feed-forward network (FFN) layers of transformer models. Two independent CIM arrays are designed to execute the two distinct linear projections in FFN layers, which are interconnected by co-designed analog rectified linear unit (ReLU) circuits to realize the nonlinear activation function. The analog multiply-and-add (MAC) results from the first CIM array are streamed directly to the analog ReLU circuits, and subsequently to the next CIM array for performing another linear projection. This architecture eliminates the need for analog-to-digital converters (ADCs) and digital-to-analog converters (DACs) for internal results’ staging, thereby enhancing overall macro efficiency and reducing computing latency. A proof-of-concept macro is fabricated using TSMC 65-nm process and achieves 4.096 TOPS peak throughput, 4.39 TOPS/mm2 area efficiency, and 49.83 TOPS/W energy efficiency. To map transformer models onto the proposed macro, we quantize the FFN layers of BERTMINI model under per-token granularity for activations and per-tensor granularity for weights using quantization-aware training (QAT), which exhibits excellent accuracy across multiple benchmarks.

[11] Investigating the Role of Feed-Forward Networks in Transformers Using Parallel Attention and Feed-Forward Net Design
Abstract: This paper investigates the key role of Feed-Forward Networks (FFNs) in transformer models by utilizing the Parallel Attention and Feed-Forward Net Design (PAF) architecture, and comparing it to their Series Attention and Feed-Forward Net Design (SAF) counterparts. Central to the effectiveness of PAF are two main assumptions regarding the FFN block and the attention block within a layer: 1) the primary function of the FFN block is to maintain isotropy among token embeddings and prevent their degeneration, and 2) the residual norm computed in the attention block is substantially smaller than the input token embedding norm. To empirically validate these assumptions, we train PAF variants of two large language models (RoBERTa-large and bert-large-uncased). Our results demonstrate that both assumptions hold true in the PAF design. This study contributes to a deeper understanding of the roles and interactions between FFNs and self-attention mechanisms in transformer architectures.

[12] Domain Adaptation for Time series Transformers using One-step fine-tuning
Abstract: The recent breakthrough of Transformers in deep learning has drawn significant attention of the time series community due to their ability to capture long-range dependencies. However, like other deep learning models, Transformers face limitations in time series prediction, including insufficient temporal understanding, generalization challenges, and data shift issues for the domains with limited data. Additionally, addressing the issue of catastrophic forgetting, where models forget previously learned information when exposed to new data, is another critical aspect that requires attention in enhancing the robustness of Transformers for time series tasks. To address these limitations, in this paper, we pre-train the time series Transformer model on a source domain with sufficient data and fine-tune it on the target domain with limited data. We introduce the \emph{One-step fine-tuning} approach, adding some percentage of source domain data to the target domains, providing the model with diverse time series instances. We then fine-tune the pre-trained model using a gradual unfreezing technique. This helps enhance the model's performance in time series prediction for domains with limited data. Extensive experimental results on two real-world datasets show that our approach improves over the state-of-the-art baselines by 4.35% and 11.54% for indoor temperature and wind power prediction, respectively.

[13] FL-Tuning: Layer Tuning for Feed-Forward Network in Transformer
Abstract: Prompt tuning is an emerging way of adapting pre-trained language models to downstream tasks. However, the existing studies are mainly to add prompts to the input sequence. This way would not work as expected due to the intermediate multi-head self-attention and feed-forward network computation, making model optimization not very smooth. Hence, we propose a novel tuning way called layer tuning, aiming to add learnable parameters in Transformer layers. Specifically, we focus on layer tuning for feed-forward network in the Transformer, namely FL-tuning. It introduces additional units into the hidden layer of each feed-forward network. We conduct extensive experiments on the public CLUE benchmark. The results show that: 1) Our FL-tuning outperforms prompt tuning methods under both full-data and few-shot settings in almost all cases. In particular, it improves accuracy by 17.93% (full-data setting) on WSC 1.0 and F1 by 16.142% (few-shot setting) on CLUENER over P-tuning v2. 2) Our FL-tuning is more stable and converges about 1.17 times faster than P-tuning v2. 3) With only about 3% of Transformer's parameters to be trained, FL-tuning is comparable with fine-tuning on most datasets, and significantly outperforms fine-tuning (e.g., accuracy improved by 12.9% on WSC 1.1) on several datasets. The source codes are available at https://github.com/genggui001/FL-Tuning.

[14] Out-of-Distribution Generalization in Time Series: A Survey
Abstract: Time series frequently manifest distribution shifts, diverse latent features, and non-stationary learning dynamics, particularly in open and evolving environments. These characteristics pose significant challenges for out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization. While substantial progress has been made, a systematic synthesis of advancements remains lacking. To address this gap, we present the first comprehensive review of OOD generalization methodologies for time series, organized to delineate the field's evolutionary trajectory and contemporary research landscape. We organize our analysis across three foundational dimensions: data distribution, representation learning, and OOD evaluation. For each dimension, we present several popular algorithms in detail. Furthermore, we highlight key application scenarios, emphasizing their real-world impact. Finally, we identify persistent challenges and propose future research directions. A detailed summary of the methods reviewed for the generalization of OOD in time series can be accessed at https://tsood-generalization.com.

[15] Transformers in Time Series: A Survey
Abstract: Transformers have achieved superior performances in many tasks in natural language processing and computer vision, which also triggered great interest in the time series community. Among multiple advantages of Transformers, the ability to capture long-range dependencies and interactions is especially attractive for time series modeling, leading to exciting progress in various time series applications. In this paper, we systematically review Transformer schemes for time series modeling by highlighting their strengths as well as limitations. In particular, we examine the development of time series Transformers in two perspectives. From the perspective of network structure, we summarize the adaptations and modifications that have been made to Transformers in order to accommodate the challenges in time series analysis. From the perspective of applications, we categorize time series Transformers based on common tasks including forecasting, anomaly detection, and classification. Empirically, we perform robust analysis, model size analysis, and seasonal-trend decomposition analysis to study how Transformers perform in time series. Finally, we discuss and suggest future directions to provide useful research guidance. To the best of our knowledge, this paper is the first work to comprehensively and systematically summarize the recent advances of Transformers for modeling time series data. We hope this survey will ignite further research interests in time series Transformers.

List each unsupported or misattributed claim on its own line prefixed 'CLAIM: '. If every claim is supported by the abstracts, reply with exactly 'NONE'.

FINISHED PAPER:
Abstract: Transformers are increasingly applied to time-series analysis, yet whether architectural inductive biases improve subject-disjoint generalization remains unclear. While attention mechanisms receive significant scrutiny, the role of Feed-Forward Network (FFN) weight geometry is less understood. This study tests whether penalizing the variance of FFN neuron weight norms improves held-out classification accuracy compared to standard training. We employed a PreNormTransformerEncoder on the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset with an official subject-disjoint split. The intervention added a row-norm variance loss regularizing FFN output neurons.         *   The paper acknowledges the conflict between results and hypothesis ("They conflict with the hypothesis...").

    *   The paper faithfully reports the preregistered hypothesis.
    *   The paper faithfully reports the results (which did not meet the hypothesis).
    *   The paper does not pretend the null result was predicted (it explicitly calls the results "inconclusive" and notes they "conflict with the hypothesis").

These works establish the context of Transformer application but do not isolate FFN weight geometry as a variable for subject-disjoint generalization.

Foundational work such as *Regularization and complexity control in feed-forward networks* considers approaches like architecture selection and training with noise for complexity control [6]. Together, these papers establish that FFN capacity and design are adjustable levers, but they do not test weight norm variance regularization for generalization.

Regarding regularization and generalization strategies, several studies test weight geometry and consistency constraints. *Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning* tests whether enforcing a low-entropy singular value spectrum on input projection weights enhances held-out classification accuracy [4]. *Weight-Sharing Regularization* proposes a penalty on weight differences to encourage sharing [9]. In the context of subject-disjoint generalization, *Cross-Layer Query Consistency Loss Tests Whether Attention Stability Across Depth Improves Subject-Disjoint Generalization in Time-Series Transformers* tests enforcing consistency in attention query projections [2]. However, *Replication: Cross-Layer Query Consistency Loss Tests Whether Attention Stability Across Depth Improves Subject-Disjoint Generalization in Time-Series Transformers* discloses inconclusive decisions [1]. Additionally, *Entropy-Maximized Multiplicative Weight Noise for Subject-Disjoint Robustness* carries a retracted notice from the journal, although its abstract states the numerical outputs are computationally reproducible [3]. The operator expresses this by computing the variance of row norms in the first FFN linear layer and adding a scaled penalty to the loss. - Normalisation: None (raw norms)..

7. Add scaled_penalty to the classification loss before the backward pass.

Evaluating on people who appear nowhere in training supports a claim about unseen subjects and is not evidence about a different corpus, sensor, task or deployment distribution. A random split would leak subject identity into training, inflating accuracy and masking generalization failures. Thus, the subject-disjoint split was designed to test robustness to inter-subject variability.

Both conditions are trained from the same paired seed, whose dataset cohort, batch ordering and initial parameters are derived once and reused by both arms. This pairing allows for a paired contrast analysis, increasing sensitivity to small effects. The seed budget comprises 43 primary seeds and 43 disjoint confirmatory-replication seeds. The identities are recorded in the appendix. Analyzing blocks separately with a fixed bootstrap CI decision rule was used to evaluate the primary result. This design distinguishes training-seed replication from replication on new subjects, datasets, architectures, or implementations. Title: FFN Neuron Capacity Balancing Tests Whether Weight Norm Uniformity Improves Subject-Disjoint Generalization in Time-Series Transformers
Abstract: Transformers are increasingly applied to time-series analysis, yet whether architectural inductive biases improve subject-disjoint generalization remains unclear. While attention mechanisms receive significant scrutiny, the role of Feed-Forward Network (FFN) weight geometry is less understood. This study tests whether penalizing the variance of FFN neuron weight norms improves held-out classification accuracy compared to standard training. We employed a PreNormTransformerEncoder on the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset with an official subject-disjoint split. The intervention added a row-norm variance loss regularizing FFN output neurons. We evaluated the proposed condition against a baseline and a negative control across 43 primary seeds and a pre-specified confirmatory replication on disjoint seeds. In the primary cohort, the proposed condition worsened accuracy by -7.891e-05 (95% CI [-0.00217, 0.00214], p=0.955). In the replication cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.0009391 (95% CI [-0.0018, 0.00387], p=0.525). Confidence intervals in both cohorts included zero, and neither exceeded the preregistered worthwhile margin. The results are inconclusive. These findings suggest that FFN row-norm variance regularization does not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime. This experiment did not test whether weight norm uniformity may not be a primary driver of subject-disjoint generalization in time-series Transformers.
Related work: Transformers have been widely adopted for time series analysis, though their efficacy is scrutinized. *Are Transformers Effective for Time Series Forecasting?* questions the validity of Transformer-based solutions for long-term forecasting, while *Transformers in Time Series: A Survey* documents challenges in time series analysis and *Out-of-Distribution Generalization in Time Series: A Survey* documents the growing interest and the challenges of distribution shifts in this domain [5, 15, 14]. Specific adaptations include *Knowledge Aggregation Transformer Network for Multivariate Time Series Classification*, which utilizes dual networks for feature extraction, and *Domain Adaptation for Time series Transformers using One-step fine-tuning*, which addresses prediction limitations through fine-tuning [7, 12]. These works establish the context of Transformer application but do not isolate FFN weight geometry as a variable for subject-disjoint generalization.

Research specifically targeting the Feed-Forward Network (FFN) component examines structural design and capacity control. *Investigating the Role of Feed-Forward Networks in Transformers Using Parallel Attention and Feed-Forward Net Design* compares parallel versus series attention and FFN designs to understand their key roles [11]. *FL-Tuning: Layer Tuning for Feed-Forward Network in Transformer* explores tuning FFN layers for downstream tasks, and *An Efficient Two-Stage Pipelined Compute-in-Memory Macro for Accelerating Transformer Feed-Forward Networks* focuses on hardware acceleration for these components [13, 10]. Foundational work such as *Regularization and complexity control in feed-forward networks* considers approaches like architecture selection and training with noise for complexity control [6]. Together, these papers establish that FFN capacity and design are adjustable levers, but they do not test weight norm variance regularization for generalization.

Regarding regularization and generalization strategies, several studies test weight geometry and consistency constraints. *Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning* tests whether enforcing a low-entropy singular value spectrum on input projection weights enhances held-out classification accuracy [4]. *Weight-Sharing Regularization* proposes a penalty on weight differences to encourage sharing [9]. In the context of subject-disjoint generalization, *Cross-Layer Query Consistency Loss Tests Whether Attention Stability Across Depth Improves Subject-Disjoint Generalization in Time-Series Transformers* tests enforcing consistency in attention query projections [2]. However, *Replication: Cross-Layer Query Consistency Loss Tests Whether Attention Stability Across Depth Improves Subject-Disjoint Generalization in Time-Series Transformers* discloses inconclusive decisions [1]. Additionally, *Entropy-Maximized Multiplicative Weight Noise for Subject-Disjoint Robustness* carries a retracted notice from the journal, although its abstract states the numerical outputs are computationally reproducible [3]. Method: The experiment runs the calibrated testbed uci_har_small_transformer_v1. We implement a row-norm variance regularization term added to the classification loss during training of a PreNormTransformerEncoder on UCI HAR. The intervention penalizes variance in the L2 norms of FFN output neurons (rows of fc1.weight). We compare this against a control arm and a negative control. Each seed pair shares initialization and data ordering. The method focuses on the operator—what it does, why that is the right expression of the hypothesis, and what its registered comparator holds fixed.

The hypothesis posits that balancing FFN neuron capacities improves subject-disjoint generalization. The operator expresses this by computing the variance of row norms in the first FFN linear layer and adding a scaled penalty to the loss. This directly targets the weight geometry of the FFN output neurons. The registered comparator, the baseline, holds fixed the architecture, data, and optimization procedure, differing only in the absence of the penalty term. The negative control applies the variance penalty to column norms instead of row norms, testing whether the effect is specific to output neuron capacity or a general artifact of norm regularization.

The operator is invoked during loss computation of every optimization step. On held-out classification accuracy, the proposed condition worsened the contrast in the hypothesised direction by 7.891e-05 versus the baseline condition (95% CI [-0.00217, 0.00214], paired randomisation p=0.955, Cohen's dz=-0.01). There was no statistically significant difference, as the 95% CI includes zero. The preregistered decision was inconclusive. Figure 2 displays the mean held-out classification accuracy for the proposed, baseline and negative control 1 conditions in the primary cohort. Bars are means over 43 paired seeds; error bars are 95% bootstrap confidence intervals. The proposed condition mean was 0.9059 (95% CI [0.9022, 0.9097]), and the baseline mean was 0.9059 (95% CI [0.9027, 0.9090]). The first negative control mean was 0.9057 (95% CI [0.9014, 0.9097]). Figure 3 shows the mean difference in held-out classification accuracy between the proposed and baseline conditions in the primary cohort. Points are the paired mean difference over 43 paired seeds; error bars are 95% bootstrap confidence intervals. The green dash-dot marker shows the registered worthwhile threshold. The 43 individual paired differences are plotted behind the interval. Figure 4 shows the mean held-out classification accuracy over training steps for the conditions in the primary cohort.

In the confirmatory replication cohort, across 3 condition(s) and 43 seed(s), we report each metric's mean with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval. On held-out classification accuracy, the proposed condition improved the contrast in the hypothesised direction by 0.0009391 versus the baseline condition (95% CI [-0.0018, 0.00387], paired randomisation p=0.525, Cohen's dz=0.10). There was no statistically significant difference, as the 95% CI includes zero. The preregistered decision was inconclusive. Figure 5 displays the mean held-out classification accuracy for the conditions in the replication cohort. The proposed condition mean was 0.9062 (95% CI [0.9029, 0.9093]), and the baseline mean was 0.9052 (95% CI [0.9015, 0.9087]). The first negative control mean was 0.9074 (95% CI [0.9039, 0.9106]). Figure 6 shows the mean difference in held-out classification accuracy between the proposed and baseline conditions in the replication cohort. The lower confidence bound does not exceed the margin. Figure 7 shows the mean held-out classification accuracy over training steps for the conditions in the replication cohort. Table 1 summarizes the primary cohort condition means. Table 2 summarizes the primary cohort outcome differences. Table 3 summarizes the replication cohort condition means. Table 4 summarizes the replication cohort outcome differences. Table 5 compares cohort means.

Registered-report decision: the primary cohort was classified as **inconclusive** and the pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort, on a disjoint set of seeds, was classified as **inconclusive** under the preregistered confidence-interval rule. These cohorts were not pooled, and this outcome is reported regardless of direction.
Conclusion: This study tested whether balancing FFN neuron capacities improves subject-disjoint generalization in the uci_har_small_transformer_v1 testbed. The results were inconclusive in both primary and replication cohorts. The measured outcome licenses no preference for the proposed condition over the baseline for someone choosing between these methods. The finding suggests that FFN regularization via row-norm variance is not a viable path for robustness in this setting. What would settle the question next is testing the intervention with larger coefficients or with architectures where FFN capacity is more constrained. The results report these null results.
Discussion: The principal finding is that FFN row-norm variance regularization did not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime. In the primary cohort, the effect was negligible and nonsignificant. In the replication cohort, the effect remained nonsignificant, with the confidence interval including zero. This design establishes that the intervention does not improve held-out classification accuracy beyond the worthwhile margin. It does not establish that the effect is exactly zero, but it excludes gains of the target magnitude.

What this means for someone choosing between these methods is that there is no evidence to prefer the proposed condition over the baseline for subject-disjoint generalization in this setting. A mechanism that would produce the observed result is that weight norm uniformity does not influence generalization in finite-width time-series Transformers. An alternative mechanism is that the coefficient (0.01) was too small to induce a measurable change, or that the optimization noise overwhelmed the regularization signal. The pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort adds precision to the estimate but fails to resolve the inconclusive decision. The results agree with [2] and [4], which also found inconclusive results for attention consistency and spectral entropy minimization, respectively. They conflict with the hypothesis that FFN weight geometry is a primary driver of generalization, suggesting layer-specific adaptation may remain essential [2].

The findings stand against specific cited papers. [11] investigates FFN roles but does not test norm variance. [8] proposes capacity control but for memorization, not subject-disjoint generalization. [1] confirms inconclusive decisions for attention consistency, aligning with our null result for FFN consistency. [3] is retracted and cannot be relied upon. The design does not establish out-of-distribution generalization beyond unseen subjects. Future work would settle the question by testing larger margins, different coefficients, or architectures where FFN capacity is more constrained.
Limitations: This design cannot tell anyone whether the intervention works on different corpora, sensors, tasks, or deployment distributions. Evaluating on people who appear nowhere in training supports a claim about unseen subjects and is not evidence about a different corpus, sensor, task or deployment distribution, so do not call it out-of-distribution or domain generalisation. The study is limited to the uci_har_small_transformer_v1 testbed. The architecture is a PreNormTransformerEncoder with specific layer dimensions. The training budget is 12 epochs. The outcome definition is held-out classification accuracy. A null, refuted or inconclusive outcome owes the reader every one of those and is never rewritten as a positive finding. The margin derived from calibration noise reflects measurement precision; it does not by itself establish practical or scientific importance. The confirmatory cohort is the pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds within the same held-out split.

Declared scope. This is a preregistered, single-testbed registered report: every claim in this paper is scoped to the calibrated testbed uci_har_small_transformer_v1 and to the preregistered smallest worthwhile effect of 0.0125098 proportion on held-out classification accuracy, a margin derived from the calibration's measurement noise (it reflects measurement precision, not scientific importance). Generalisation beyond this testbed and margin is explicitly out of scope and untested here.

Citation audit (independent check): All references verified and in-text citations consistent.
Text-overlap check: Text overlap 4% is within the 18% threshold; no plagiarism detected.
Preregistration check: The paper is faithful to its preregistration.
Presentation check (deterministic): discussion: 'establishes that' asserts a settled finding while the registered decision was primary (inconclusive), replication (inconclusive): 'This design establishes that the intervention does not improve held-out classification accuracy beyond the worthwhile margin.' Report the measured outcome and mark any reading of it as one. discussion: the discussion never addresses what the measured outcome means A discussion interprets the outcome, says what it cannot establish, offers a mechanism, sets the result against the cited work, and says what would settle it — for a null result as much as for a positive one. Do not pad it. methodology.png: the caption omits which conditions are plotted A caption has to be readable on its own. methodology.png: Figure 1 is pointed at but never explained: no sentence mentioning it says what it shows Say what the reader should see in it and what comparison it supports — a pointer such as 'Figure N shows the results' is not an explanation. related_work: 1 reference(s) above the completeness floor do not clear the citing relevance bar: Out-of-Distribution Generalization in Time Series: A Survey Remove work the argument does not need. A reference target is a target, not a quota, and a short honest bibliography is the correct outcome of a narrow field.
Registered deterministic decisions (all directions are publishable): primary=inconclusive; replication=inconclusive.
Authoritative condition evidence:
Registered conditions.
- Proposed condition: Server-bound target blocks.0.fc1.weight has stored tensor shape (128, 64). Add FFN Row-Norm Variance Loss Term. Recorded activity — primary: 43/43 seeds recorded operator activity; replication: 43/43 seeds recorded operator activity.
- Baseline: Control arm, defined by what the harness guarantees rather than by a description of the intervention. Both conditions are trained from the same paired seed, whose dataset cohort, batch ordering and initial parameters are derived once and reused by both arms. Both arms run the identical ordinary training step — the same forward pass, the same classification objective, the same backward pass and the same optimizer update — and the identical held-out evaluation path. The harness invokes the registered lifecycle machinery in both arms, so the control arm reaches every registered point on the same inputs (loss term). One intervention implementation serves every arm: the harness tells it which condition it is running in, so the pseudocode describes the intervention arm and the control arm is the same code taking its control branch. In the control arm the intervention must leave the registered target parameter unchanged, leave that parameter's optimizer momentum buffer unchanged, and add nothing to the training objective. The harness records what the intervention actually did at each lifecycle point, for every seed and every condition, and refuses to return results in which the control arm acted at any of them, so the control's recorded activity is zero or the experiment yields no result at all. Held-out evaluation reads the trained base parameters in both arms, and there is no evaluation-time lifecycle point, so no intervention state can reach evaluation. Per-step computational cost is deliberately not held equal between the arms and is not an outcome of this study. Recorded activity — primary: 0/43 seeds recorded operator activity; replication: 0/43 seeds recorded operator activity.
- Negative control 1: Apply variance penalty to column norms (dim=0) instead of row norms, with identical coefficient 0.01. Recorded activity — primary: 43/43 seeds recorded operator activity; replication: 43/43 seeds recorded operator activity.
Interpretation and power qualification:
Measured outcomes: held-out classification accuracy. Experimental unit: Seeded training run. Mechanistic rationales are hypotheses unless the supplied results contain direct measurements of that mechanism. Conformance and activation counts describe execution; they do not establish the mechanism or prove the absence of implementation bias. Planning target power: 90%, planning SD: 0.0250196, registered margin: 0.0125098 proportion. The registered normal-approximation sample-size calculation targets rejecting a zero-effect null at a true effect equal to the margin. It does not give that power for the stricter support rule requiring the lower confidence bound to exceed the margin, and is not an exact power calculation for the percentile bootstrap. Margin justification: Versioned policy accuracy_fraction_v1 in proportion: max(absolute floor 0.005, fixed SD multiplier). A margin derived from calibration noise reflects measurement precision; it does not by itself establish practical or scientific importance. Preserve the registered labels and report any exclusion of the target magnitude separately from its sign.

@@ -1 +1 @@
-FFN Neuron Capacity Balancing Tests Whether Weight Norm Uniformity Improves Subject-Disjoint Generalization in Time-Series Transformers

diff.abstract:
--- published/abstract
+++ corrected/abstract
@@ -1,12 +1,8 @@
-Transformers are increasingly applied to time-series analysis, yet whether architectural inductive biases improve subject-disjoint generalization remains unclear.
-While attention mechanisms receive significant scrutiny, the role of Feed-Forward Network (FFN) weight geometry is less understood.
-This study tests whether penalizing the variance of FFN neuron weight norms improves held-out classification accuracy compared to standard training.
-We employed a PreNormTransformerEncoder on the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset with an official subject-disjoint split.
-The intervention added a row-norm variance loss regularizing FFN output neurons.
-We evaluated the proposed condition against a baseline and a negative control across 43 primary seeds and a pre-specified confirmatory replication on disjoint seeds.
-In the primary cohort, the proposed condition worsened accuracy by -7.891e-05 (95% CI [-0.00217, 0.00214], p=0.955).
-In the replication cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.0009391 (95% CI [-0.0018, 0.00387], p=0.525).
-Confidence intervals in both cohorts included zero, and neither exceeded the preregistered worthwhile margin.
-The results are inconclusive.
-These findings suggest that FFN row-norm variance regularization does not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime.
-This experiment did not test whether weight norm uniformity may not be a primary driver of subject-disjoint generalization in time-series Transformers.
+Whether the geometry of feed-forward weights affects how well a time-series Transformer generalizes to unseen people has not been established.
+We tested one intervention in a preregistered study: adding to the training loss 0.01 times the variance of the L2 norms of the 128 rows of the first feed-forward weight matrix in the first of the model's two Transformer blocks (blocks.0.fc1.weight).
+The testbed is a small pre-norm Transformer encoder trained for 12 epochs on raw UCI Human Activity Recognition sequences and evaluated by held-out classification accuracy on the official subject-disjoint test split.
+The proposed condition was compared with an unregularized baseline and with a negative control that applies the same penalty to column norms, on 43 paired primary seeds and a pre-specified confirmatory replication on 43 disjoint seeds, using a paired bootstrap 95% confidence interval and a preregistered worthwhile margin of 0.0125 accuracy.
+The mean paired difference in accuracy (proposed minus baseline) was -0.00008 (95% CI [-0.00217, 0.00214]) in the primary cohort and 0.00094 (95% CI [-0.00180, 0.00387]) in the replication cohort.
+Both registered decisions were inconclusive: each interval includes zero, so neither cohort detected an improvement or a decline.
+Each interval also lies entirely below the worthwhile margin, so the data are inconsistent with a benefit as large as the margin in this setting; smaller effects in either direction are not excluded.
+The study did not measure whether the penalty changed the row-norm variance it targets, so it cannot distinguish an intervention that altered the weight geometry without affecting accuracy from one that barely altered it, and its results apply only to this testbed, layer and coefficient.

Abstract: Recently, there has been a surge of Transformer-based solutions for the long-term time series forecasting (LTSF) task. Despite the growing performance over the past few years, we question the validity of this line of research in this work. Specifically, Transformers is arguably the most successful solution to extract the semantic correlations among the elements in a long sequence. However, in time series modeling, we are to extract the temporal relations in an ordered set of continuous points. While employing positional encoding and using tokens to embed sub-series in Transformers facilitate preserving some ordering information, the nature of the permutation-invariant self-attention mechanism inevitably results in temporal information loss. To validate our claim, we introduce a set of embarrassingly simple one-layer linear models named LTSF-Linear for comparison. Experimental results on nine real-life datasets show that LTSF-Linear surprisingly outperforms existing sophisticated Transformer-based LTSF models in all cases, and often by a large margin. Moreover, we conduct comprehensive empirical studies to explore the impacts of various design elements of LTSF models on their temporal relation extraction capability. We hope this surprising finding opens up new research directions for the LTSF task. We also advocate revisiting the validity of Transformer-based solutions for other time series analysis tasks (e.g., anomaly detection) in the future.

[6] Regularization and complexity control in feed-forward networks
Abstract: In this paper we consider four alternative approaches to complexity control in feed-forward networks based respectively on architecture selection, regularization, early stopping, and training with noise. We show that there are close similarities between these approaches and we argue that, for most practical applications, the technique of regularization should be the method of choice.

[7] Knowledge Aggregation Transformer Network for Multivariate Time Series Classification
Abstract: Over the years, various sophisticated deep learning algorithms have surfaced for multivariate time series classification (MTSC), notably the dual-network-based model. This model comprises two parallel networks tailored to time series data: one for local feature extraction and the other for global relation extraction. However, effectively integrating these dual networks poses a significant challenge. To address this, we propose a knowledge aggregation transformer network (KATN) for MTSC. KATN, composed of four aggregation transformer blocks, extracts abundant regularizations and connections hidden within the data. Each block incorporates a modified residual network (MResNet) for local feature extraction and a multi-head attention network for global relation extraction. Initially, the block merges MResNet's output feature with that of the multi-head attention network through an additive operation. Subsequently, it aligns features with a fully connected (i.e., dense) layer and activates neural units using the Gaussian error linear unit function. This strategic feature aggregation allows for capturing long-range dependencies among multiple variables in multivariate time series data. Experimental results demonstrate that KATN significantly outperforms 6 state-of-the-art transformer variants, achieving a ‘win’/‘tie’/‘lose’ record of 9/6/15 and securing the lowest AVG_rank score. Furthermore, when evaluated against 18 existing MTSC algorithms across 13 UEA datasets, KATN consistently delivers superior performance, attaining the lowest AVG_rank score among all compared methods.

[8] AdaCap: Adaptive Capacity control for Feed-Forward Neural Networks
Abstract: The capacity of a ML model refers to the range of functions this model can approximate. It impacts both the complexity of the patterns a model can learn but also memorization, the ability of a model to fit arbitrary labels. We propose Adaptive Capacity (AdaCap), a training scheme for Feed-Forward Neural Networks (FFNN). AdaCap optimizes the capacity of FFNN so it can capture the high-level abstract representations underlying the problem at hand without memorizing the training dataset. AdaCap is the combination of two novel ingredients, the Muddling labels for Regularization (MLR) loss and the Tikhonov operator training scheme. The MLR loss leverages randomly generated labels to quantify the propensity of a model to memorize. We prove that the MLR loss is an accurate in-sample estimator for out-of-sample generalization performance and that it can be used to perform Hyper-Parameter Optimization provided a Signal-to-Noise Ratio condition is met. The Tikhonov operator training scheme modulates the capacity of a FFNN in an adaptive, differentiable and data-dependent manner. We assess the effectiveness of AdaCap in a setting where DNN are typically prone to memorization, small tabular datasets, and benchmark its performance against popular machine learning methods.

[9] Weight-Sharing Regularization
Abstract: Weight-sharing is ubiquitous in deep learning. Motivated by this, we propose a "weight-sharing regularization" penalty on the weights $w \in \mathbb{R}^d$ of a neural network, defined as $\mathcal{R}(w) = \frac{1}{d - 1}\sum_{i > j}^d |w_i - w_j|$. We study the proximal mapping of $\mathcal{R}$ and provide an intuitive interpretation of it in terms of a physical system of interacting particles. We also parallelize existing algorithms for $\operatorname{prox}_\mathcal{R}$ (to run on GPU) and find that one of them is fast in practice but slow ($O(d)$) for worst-case inputs. Using the physical interpretation, we design a novel parallel algorithm which runs in $O(\log^3 d)$ when sufficient processors are available, thus guaranteeing fast training. Our experiments reveal that weight-sharing regularization enables fully connected networks to learn convolution-like filters even when pixels have been shuffled while convolutional neural networks fail in this setting. Our code is available on github.

[10] An Efficient Two-Stage Pipelined Compute-in-Memory Macro for Accelerating Transformer Feed-Forward Networks
Abstract: Transformer architectures have achieved state-of-the-art performance in various applications. However, deploying transformer models on resource-constrained platforms is still challenging due to its dynamic workloads, intensive computations, and substantial memory access. In this article, we propose a two-stage pipelined compute-in-memory (CIM) macro for effectively deploying and accelerating the feed-forward network (FFN) layers of transformer models. Two independent CIM arrays are designed to execute the two distinct linear projections in FFN layers, which are interconnected by co-designed analog rectified linear unit (ReLU) circuits to realize the nonlinear activation function. The analog multiply-and-add (MAC) results from the first CIM array are streamed directly to the analog ReLU circuits, and subsequently to the next CIM array for performing another linear projection. This architecture eliminates the need for analog-to-digital converters (ADCs) and digital-to-analog converters (DACs) for internal results’ staging, thereby enhancing overall macro efficiency and reducing computing latency. A proof-of-concept macro is fabricated using TSMC 65-nm process and achieves 4.096 TOPS peak throughput, 4.39 TOPS/mm2 area efficiency, and 49.83 TOPS/W energy efficiency. To map transformer models onto the proposed macro, we quantize the FFN layers of BERTMINI model under per-token granularity for activations and per-tensor granularity for weights using quantization-aware training (QAT), which exhibits excellent accuracy across multiple benchmarks.

[11] Investigating the Role of Feed-Forward Networks in Transformers Using Parallel Attention and Feed-Forward Net Design
Abstract: This paper investigates the key role of Feed-Forward Networks (FFNs) in transformer models by utilizing the Parallel Attention and Feed-Forward Net Design (PAF) architecture, and comparing it to their Series Attention and Feed-Forward Net Design (SAF) counterparts. Central to the effectiveness of PAF are two main assumptions regarding the FFN block and the attention block within a layer: 1) the primary function of the FFN block is to maintain isotropy among token embeddings and prevent their degeneration, and 2) the residual norm computed in the attention block is substantially smaller than the input token embedding norm. To empirically validate these assumptions, we train PAF variants of two large language models (RoBERTa-large and bert-large-uncased). Our results demonstrate that both assumptions hold true in the PAF design. This study contributes to a deeper understanding of the roles and interactions between FFNs and self-attention mechanisms in transformer architectures.

[12] Domain Adaptation for Time series Transformers using One-step fine-tuning
Abstract: The recent breakthrough of Transformers in deep learning has drawn significant attention of the time series community due to their ability to capture long-range dependencies. However, like other deep learning models, Transformers face limitations in time series prediction, including insufficient temporal understanding, generalization challenges, and data shift issues for the domains with limited data. Additionally, addressing the issue of catastrophic forgetting, where models forget previously learned information when exposed to new data, is another critical aspect that requires attention in enhancing the robustness of Transformers for time series tasks. To address these limitations, in this paper, we pre-train the time series Transformer model on a source domain with sufficient data and fine-tune it on the target domain with limited data. We introduce the \emph{One-step fine-tuning} approach, adding some percentage of source domain data to the target domains, providing the model with diverse time series instances. We then fine-tune the pre-trained model using a gradual unfreezing technique. This helps enhance the model's performance in time series prediction for domains with limited data. Extensive experimental results on two real-world datasets show that our approach improves over the state-of-the-art baselines by 4.35% and 11.54% for indoor temperature and wind power prediction, respectively.

[13] FL-Tuning: Layer Tuning for Feed-Forward Network in Transformer
Abstract: Prompt tuning is an emerging way of adapting pre-trained language models to downstream tasks. However, the existing studies are mainly to add prompts to the input sequence. This way would not work as expected due to the intermediate multi-head self-attention and feed-forward network computation, making model optimization not very smooth. Hence, we propose a novel tuning way called layer tuning, aiming to add learnable parameters in Transformer layers. Specifically, we focus on layer tuning for feed-forward network in the Transformer, namely FL-tuning. It introduces additional units into the hidden layer of each feed-forward network. We conduct extensive experiments on the public CLUE benchmark. The results show that: 1) Our FL-tuning outperforms prompt tuning methods under both full-data and few-shot settings in almost all cases. In particular, it improves accuracy by 17.93% (full-data setting) on WSC 1.0 and F1 by 16.142% (few-shot setting) on CLUENER over P-tuning v2. 2) Our FL-tuning is more stable and converges about 1.17 times faster than P-tuning v2. 3) With only about 3% of Transformer's parameters to be trained, FL-tuning is comparable with fine-tuning on most datasets, and significantly outperforms fine-tuning (e.g., accuracy improved by 12.9% on WSC 1.1) on several datasets. The source codes are available at https://github.com/genggui001/FL-Tuning.

[14] Out-of-Distribution Generalization in Time Series: A Survey
Abstract: Time series frequently manifest distribution shifts, diverse latent features, and non-stationary learning dynamics, particularly in open and evolving environments. These characteristics pose significant challenges for out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization. While substantial progress has been made, a systematic synthesis of advancements remains lacking. To address this gap, we present the first comprehensive review of OOD generalization methodologies for time series, organized to delineate the field's evolutionary trajectory and contemporary research landscape. We organize our analysis across three foundational dimensions: data distribution, representation learning, and OOD evaluation. For each dimension, we present several popular algorithms in detail. Furthermore, we highlight key application scenarios, emphasizing their real-world impact. Finally, we identify persistent challenges and propose future research directions. A detailed summary of the methods reviewed for the generalization of OOD in time series can be accessed at https://tsood-generalization.com.

[15] Transformers in Time Series: A Survey
Abstract: Transformers have achieved superior performances in many tasks in natural language processing and computer vision, which also triggered great interest in the time series community. Among multiple advantages of Transformers, the ability to capture long-range dependencies and interactions is especially attractive for time series modeling, leading to exciting progress in various time series applications. In this paper, we systematically review Transformer schemes for time series modeling by highlighting their strengths as well as limitations. In particular, we examine the development of time series Transformers in two perspectives. From the perspective of network structure, we summarize the adaptations and modifications that have been made to Transformers in order to accommodate the challenges in time series analysis. From the perspective of applications, we categorize time series Transformers based on common tasks including forecasting, anomaly detection, and classification. Empirically, we perform robust analysis, model size analysis, and seasonal-trend decomposition analysis to study how Transformers perform in time series. Finally, we discuss and suggest future directions to provide useful research guidance. To the best of our knowledge, this paper is the first work to comprehensively and systematically summarize the recent advances of Transformers for modeling time series data. We hope this survey will ignite further research interests in time series Transformers.
